A way that can be told as a way is not the constant Dao. A name that can be given as a name is not the constant name.  Nameless: the beginning of heaven and earth. Named: the mother of the ten thousand things.  So: always without wanting, to watch its fineness; always with wanting, to watch its edges.  These two come out together and differ in name. Alike, call them dark. Dark, and darker still: the gate of all fineness. The first line has six characters, and three of them are 道. The first is a noun: a way, a road. The second is a verb. As a verb 道 can mean “to speak, to tell”; an old song in the Book of Odes says of palace gossip 不可道也, “it cannot be told”. It can also mean “to lead along a road” (the Analects uses it for guiding a state). The third 道 is the noun again, now with 常 in front of it. So the line hears itself: a way that can be way-ed is not the constant way. English must pick “told” or “walked” or “followed”. The Chinese picks nothing. The line also does what it describes: it names Dao and, in the same breath, takes the name back. Which verb did you hear first?

Carrying the bodily soul, holding the One in the arms: can there be no parting? Gathering the breath to the utmost softness: can one be as an infant? Washing clean the dark mirror: can it be without a flaw? Caring for the state, ordering the people: can it be without cleverness? Heaven’s gate opens and shuts: can one take the hen’s part? Bright and clear, reaching the four quarters: can it be without forcing?  Giving them life, rearing them. Giving life, not owning; acting, not leaning on it; raising, not ruling: this is called the dark power. The first part is six questions on one frame: four characters that name a practice, then 能 … 乎, “can … ?”. The Chinese has no “you”. It does not say who is asked, and it does not say that the answer is yes. Legge made the first three into statements about a “he”; many modern versions write “Can you…?”. Both are additions. We mostly write “can there be” and “can it be”, and twice English forces “one”. This is stiff, and it keeps the question open to anyone, the speaker too. The six run in an order: the soul, the breath, the mirror of the mind, then the state, the gate, and knowledge of the four quarters. The first three face inward and the last three outward. The word 能 has a surprise in it. The Shuowen says that it was first the name of an animal like a bear. See the second plate.

Cut off sagehood, throw away cleverness: the people gain a hundredfold. Cut off humaneness, throw away right conduct: the people go back to devotion and tender care. Cut off skill, throw away profit: robbers and bandits, there are none.  These three, as ornament, are not enough. So let there be something to fasten to: show the undyed silk, hold the uncarved wood; less of what is private, fewer wants. The first word of the passage, used three times, is a weaver’s word. The Shuowen defines 絕 as 斷絲也, “to cut silk thread”, and reads the graph as 糸, silk, with 刀, a knife, and 卩. To 絕 is to sever a line that was continuous: a thread, a road, a family with no heir, a friendship. It is sudden and final; a cut thread is not “reduced”. Passage 14 ended with a thread to follow, the lead thread of Dao; this passage begins with threads to cut. The partner verb, 棄, is as hard. English “renounce”, “give up”, or “abandon” are words of the will and the conscience. The Chinese verbs are acts of the hand. Note also what is cut. In each pair it is the thing that the schools of the age praised most.

Know the cock, keep to the hen: be the ravine of all under heaven. Be the ravine of all under heaven, and the constant de does not leave. Go back again to the infant.  Know the white, keep to the black: be the pattern of all under heaven. Be the pattern of all under heaven, and the constant de does not go wrong. Go back again to what has no limit.  Know honour, keep to disgrace: be the valley of all under heaven, and the constant de is then enough. Go back again to the uncarved wood.  Uncarved wood, split up, becomes vessels. The sage uses them and becomes chief of the officers. So the great cutting does not sever. Three stanzas use one frame: 知其 X，守其 Y. 知 is to know, and in old usage also to be in charge of, to have mastery of. 守 is to guard a post; the Shuowen glosses it 守官也, “to keep an office”, a hand of duty under a roof. So the frame does not say “choose Y, reject X”. The person in these lines has the cock’s strength, the white, and the honour, and knows them from inside. Then that person takes up a post at the other pole. A dualist reading wants a good side and a bad side. The text wants both in one person, with the weight set low. Our verbs are commands, “know, keep”, because English needs a form; the Chinese has no subject and no mood, and can as well be read “one who knows the cock and keeps to the hen is the ravine”.

The Dao is constant in not-doing, and nothing is left undone.  If lords and kings can keep to it, the ten thousand things will change of themselves. Changed, and wanting stirs: I will weigh it down with the nameless uncarved wood.  The nameless uncarved wood: that too will be without wanting. Not wanting, and so still: all under heaven will settle of itself. 無為 is “without 為”, and 為 is a wide verb: to do, to make, to act as, to act for a purpose. The phrase does not mean idleness. A river does much and does not 為. The sense is: no action that is forced on things from outside, by a will with a plan. “Non-action” sounds like a withdrawal; “inaction” sounds like a fault. We write “not-doing” and ask you to hear “not-forcing”. The line does not tell anyone to practice it. It says that the Dao is so, 常, constantly. Wang Bi glosses the four characters with three: 順自然也, “it follows that which is so of itself”. Notice that the pinned text divides the sentence after 為, in the middle of the paradox, as a breath divides it when it is read aloud.

When the world has Dao, running horses are turned back to dung the fields. When the world has no Dao, war horses are born at the outskirts.  No calamity is greater than not to know enough; no fault is greater than the wish to get. So the enough of know-enough is always enough. 天下 is “under heaven”: the whole known world, the Zhou realm and its states. 有道, “has the Way”, was a common political phrase of the time, and it did not belong to the Daoists. Confucius uses it often. When the world has the Way, he says, show yourself; when it does not, stay hidden. And: when the world has the Way, rites, music, and campaigns of war come from the Son of Heaven alone. For such speakers 有道 means that the realm is in order and under right rule; 無道 means the age of usurpers. The Laozi takes the phrase that everyone used and gives it one test only: look at the horses. English versions write that the Dao “prevails”, a word of contest. The Chinese verb is 有, to have, as a field has water.

One who holds de within, thick and deep, is like a red child. Wasps, scorpions, vipers, snakes do not sting. Fierce beasts do not seize. Clawed birds do not strike.  Bones weak, sinews soft, yet the grip is firm. Not yet knowing the joining of female and male, yet fully roused: essence at its peak. Howls all day and is not hoarse: harmony at its peak.  Knowing harmony is named the constant. Knowing the constant is named clear sight. Adding to life is named an omen. The heart-mind driving the breath is named forcing.  A thing in its prime then grows old. Call this not the Dao. What is not the Dao ends early. 含 has 口, a mouth, at the bottom, and 今 above it for the sound. The Shuowen says 嗛也, “to hold in the mouth”. It is the verb for a thing kept behind closed lips and not swallowed and not spoken: a sweet, a sip of water, a word that is not said. So 含德 is not “to have virtue” as a person has a medal. It is 德 kept in, unshown, as a baby’s strength is all inside. 厚 is “thick”; the Shuowen explains it from the land, 山陵之厚也, “the thickness of hills”. The same verb named a funeral custom: a piece of jade, a 含, was put in the mouth of the dead. And the silk texts are reported to add 者 after 厚, which makes the subject plain: “the one who…”; our “one who” follows that, and our “thick and deep” is two words for the one word 厚. What do you hold in the mouth and not say?

What lies still is easy to hold. What shows no sign yet is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to break apart. What is fine is easy to scatter.  Act on it while it is not yet there. Order it while it is not yet in disorder.  A tree that fills the arms’ embrace is born from the tip of a hair. A terrace of nine tiers rises from heaped earth. A journey of a thousand li begins under the foot.  Who acts on it ruins it. Who grips it loses it. So the sage does not force, and so ruins nothing; does not grip, and so loses nothing.  People at their work constantly ruin it when it is nearly done. Be as careful of the end as of the start: then no work is ruined.  So the sage desires not to desire and does not prize hard-to-get goods; learns not to learn and goes back to what the many pass by, to assist the self-so of the ten thousand things, and does not dare to act. 未兆 is “not yet 兆”. The word comes from divination. A diviner of the Shang and Zhou courts put a hot point to a turtle shell or an ox bone. The shell cracked, and the diviner read the cracks as the answer. Those cracks are 兆. The Shuowen enters the word under a fuller graph, 𠧞, with the part 卜, and says 灼龜坼也: “the splits of a scorched turtle shell”. So the line does not say “before it begins”. It says: before the shell has cracked, while no sign can be read at all. The sage of this passage works earlier than the diviner. A diviner waits for the crack. What do you wait for before you act?

Courage in daring: killing. Courage in not daring: life. Of these two, sometimes benefit, sometimes harm.  What heaven hates: who knows the reason? So even the sage finds it hard.  The way of heaven: it does not contend, and is good at winning; does not speak, and is good at answering; does not summon, and things come of themselves; slack, and good at planning.  Heaven’s net is wide, wide. Its mesh is loose, and it loses nothing. The Shuowen gives 勇 a definition of one word: 气也, “it is breath”. 气 is the old way to write 氣: the breath, the vapour that rises, the force that moves a body. So courage is not first a moral quality. It is a surge in the chest. The graph has 力, strength, below, and 甬 above for the sound. The line does not praise this surge and does not blame it. It asks where the surge goes: into 敢, daring, or into 不敢, not daring. The second is still 勇. Passage 67 gives the source that the Laozi trusts: 慈故能勇, “from care comes the ability to be brave”. Where in your body do you feel the breath rise before a bold act?
